principles.text: There is no substitute for hours. Time in the saddle is the best predictor of getting good.
Use AI to research and learn, but stay the one writing and reviewing the code.
When code gets cheap, the right line of code gets more valuable. Good engineering decisions compound.
Learn Vim motions and know your tools. Command over your whole system beats just using an editor.
Bet that you can solve problems you don't know yet, and take the job nobody else wants.

sampleQA.question: Should I use Copilot or AI agents while I'm learning to code?

answer.text: He turned off Copilot and realized he didn't know Go. He only knew how to use Copilot to write Go.
Use it only for code you already know how to write. If the output surprises you, or it solves something you can't, skip it.
Ask the AI how to do each step, then program it yourself. Don't avoid hard things because you think AI may automate them.

sampleQA.question: How long does it take to get good enough to get hired?

answer.text: There is no six-month path to a six-figure job. Treat it as a marathon of about ten years.
At first you are bad and it hurts, then hour after hour makes you slowly better.
Work hard, get smart. To learn a language, read the whole reference first, then build real things.
Always learn Vim motions. The editor itself is optional, but try it long enough to understand it.
The real point is knowing your tools: grep, find, xargs, awk and tmux solve problems your editor shouldn't have to.
Cap the tinkering. He edits his Neovim config about once a year.
